issues.legal_issue: A non-party may seek discretionary appellate review of a criminal acquittal when the case presents a prima facie concern of serious public interest and the State has not appealed.
material_facts: The State had not challenged the order that quashed the charges.
The person seeking review was not the original complainant, who had died.
The allegations concerned the alleged acquisition of government land through manipulated records and forged documents, and the Court found a prima facie case.
The appeal was brought in the larger public interest.
issues.conclusion: The preliminary objection to the non-party's standing was rejected, and the appeal was entertained.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers a wide discretionary power to interfere in suitable cases rather than a general right of appeal. Although that power must be exercised with strict vigilance, standing is not categorically restricted to parties; a wider understanding may be necessary where there is no independent prosecution authority readily accessible to citizens. The Court relied on PSR Sadhanantham v. Arunachalam, (1980) 3 SCC 141.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_by_nonparty and state_did_not_appeal and serious_public_interest_allegations and prima_facie_case

predicates.criminal_appeal_by_nonparty: A person who was not a party to the criminal proceeding seeks appellate review.
predicates.state_did_not_appeal: The State did not appeal the decision challenged by the non-party.
predicates.serious_public_interest_allegations: The allegations concern serious wrongdoing affecting a public interest.
predicates.prima_facie_case: The material before the Court indicates a prima facie case warranting consideration.

issues.definition: When a non-party seeks review of a criminal decision that the State has not appealed, serious public-interest allegations supported by a prima facie case may permit the appeal to be entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court reviewing an order framing a criminal charge must not reappraise evidence to quash the charge where the prosecution material discloses a prima facie case.
material_facts: The trial court framed charges after considering the prosecution case.
The High Court, in revision, assessed the evidence and made findings about the accused's involvement in the alleged manipulation of records and transfers of land.
The alleged conduct involved connected acts, including obtaining powers of attorney and alleged fraudulent sales, as well as alleged fabricated wills.
The Supreme Court found a prima facie case and concluded that the High Court had overstepped its revisional jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not reappraise the evidence to quash the charges; the order framing charges was confirmed.
issues.legal_principle: At the charge stage, the court considers whether the prosecution material discloses a prima facie case; it does not conduct a roving or fishing inquiry. Revisional powers cannot be exercised routinely to appreciate evidence as a trial or appellate court would. Intervention may be warranted where a legal bar prevents proceedings or where the allegations, taken at face value, do not constitute the charged offence. The Court relied on Munna Devi v. State of Rajasthan, (2001) 9 SCC 631, and referred to State of Orissa v. Debendra Nath Padhi, (2005) 1 SCC 568.

predicates.criminal_revision_of_charge_order: A revisional court is reviewing an order framing a criminal charge.
predicates.prima_facie_prosecution_material: The prosecution material discloses a prima facie case against the accused.
predicates.revisional_court_reappraises_evidence: The revisional court assesses the evidence as though deciding the merits of the case.

issues.definition: In a revision against a charge order, where the prosecution material discloses a prima facie case, the revisional court may not quash the charge by reappraising the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A refusal to adjourn charge proceedings to permit a change of counsel does not violate the accused's right to counsel where the accused has been represented and the existing counsel has argued the case.
material_facts: The accused was represented by counsel over numerous hearings in the charge proceedings.
That counsel appeared for the accused and her husband and advanced arguments on the charge.
The request to change counsel was made at a late stage after the existing counsel had argued and sought further time.
The Supreme Court found that the request was a dilatory tactic and that the accused had not been denied representation by counsel of her choice.
issues.conclusion: The refusal to adjourn did not violate the accused's right to be defended by a lawyer of her choice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 303 of the Code of Criminal Procedure recognizes an accused person's right to be defended by a pleader of choice, and Article 22(1) of the Constitution protects the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner. On the facts, the Court found no violation of either guarantee.

rule.if: criminal_charge_proceeding and accused_previously_represented and existing_counsel_argued_case and late_change_request_would_delay_proceedings

predicates.criminal_charge_proceeding: The proceeding is at the stage of considering or framing criminal charges.
predicates.accused_previously_represented: The accused has been represented by counsel during the proceedings.
predicates.existing_counsel_argued_case: The counsel already representing the accused has advanced arguments on the matter.
predicates.late_change_request_would_delay_proceedi: The request to change counsel is made late and would delay the proceedings.

issues.definition: During criminal charge proceedings, where the accused has been represented and existing counsel has argued, refusing a late change-of-counsel adjournment that would delay the case does not violate the right to counsel.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal case should not be transferred on an unsupported apprehension of an unfair trial without concrete material supporting that apprehension.
material_facts: The accused sought transfer on the ground that she apprehended she would not receive a fair trial in the court handling the case.
The trial court had granted numerous hearing dates and refused further adjournment only after concluding that the accused was seeking delay and that her counsel had argued the case.
The Supreme Court found no material substantiating the apprehension of an unfair trial.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have transferred the case; the apprehension was baseless on the material presented.
issues.legal_principle: A transfer should not be ordered merely on a party's say-so. A very strong case based on concrete material must be made out before a criminal case is transferred on the ground of apprehended unfairness.

predicates.criminal_case_transfer_request: A party requests transfer of a criminal case to another court.
predicates.apprehension_of_unfair_trial: The party claims to apprehend that the trial will not be fair in the current court.
predicates.no_concrete_supporting_material: The party provides no concrete material substantiating the claimed apprehension.

issues.definition: A request to transfer a criminal case based on an apprehension of unfairness is not justified when that apprehension lacks concrete supporting material.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court should not quash charges against accused persons whose charges were not challenged by the party seeking revision.
material_facts: The accused sought revision of the order framing charges against her.
The High Court quashed the charges not only against that accused but also against the other accused.
The Supreme Court noted that the other accused had not sought that relief.
issues.conclusion: The High Court acted improperly by quashing charges against all accused when the revision request did not seek that relief.
issues.legal_principle: A court exercising revisional jurisdiction should not go beyond the scope of the relief sought by the party before it. The Court found the reliance on Bimal Chand Dhandhia v. State, 1976 Cri LJ 1594, misplaced because that case concerned a failure to follow the legally established procedure in framing charges.

predicates.criminal_revision_by_one_accused: One accused seeks revision of an order in a criminal case.
predicates.charges_of_other_accused_not_challenged: The charges against other accused persons are not challenged in the revision.
predicates.revisional_court_quashes_other_accused_c: The revisional court quashes charges against those other accused persons.

issues.definition: When one accused seeks revision and the charges against other accused persons are not challenged, the revisional court must not quash those unchallenged charges.

issues.legal_issue: A court remanding a case for a procedural hearing should leave the merits open rather than express findings likely to influence the trial court.
material_facts: The High Court set aside the charge order in part on the ground that the accused had been denied an opportunity to be heard and remanded the matter.
While doing so, the High Court expressed the view that there was no prima facie case against the accused.
The Supreme Court concluded that the merits-based observations frustrated the remand and were likely to influence the trial court.
issues.conclusion: If the High Court remanded the matter because the accused lacked an opportunity to be heard, it should have stopped there and left the merits for the trial court.
issues.legal_principle: A court ordering a procedural remand should not express a strong opinion on the merits that may influence the court conducting the further proceedings or frustrate the purpose of the remand.

predicates.criminal_case_remanded_for_procedural_he: A criminal case is remanded so that a party may receive a procedural hearing.
predicates.remanding_court_expresses_merits_view: The court ordering the remand expresses a view on the merits of the criminal case.

issues.definition: When a criminal case is remanded for a procedural hearing, the remanding court must leave the merits open if it has expressed a merits view.
